title: Episodic lease orchestrator and immediate-fallback capacity controller
author: Evan Calder
release_notes: Introduces an episodic lease allocator to provide short-duration burst capacity with an immediate fallback path; adds metrics for lease consumption, fallback activations, and headroom accounting. Backward-compatible; opt-in behind config flag.
description:
Context and motivation:
We frequently see short, high-intensity spikes (burst windows) that are costly to service with long-lived reservations. Existing warm pools and soft-burst credits reduce cost but can be slow to react at the sub-minute granularity we need for certain tenant workloads (video-summarization, nightly batch-query fans). This PR introduces an "episodic lease" concept: lightweight, short-duration leases allocated from a small dedicated reservoir to service micro-bursts with an immediate fallback controller that routes to compatible model variants or lower-cost regions when leases are exhausted. Goals: reduce tail latency for bursts while keeping long-term reserved footprint small, and provide clear telemetry for burst economics and SLA adherence.

What this changes (high level):
- Episodic lease allocator: negotiates short leases (typically 10s-90s) per-tenant with configurable max concurrency and per-epoch caps; leases decrement real-time and are auto-reconciled when nodes are preempted.
- Immediate-fallback controller: when a request cannot acquire an episodic lease, it consults a prioritized fallback graph (local spare pool > secondary region > quantized model variant) and issues a routed request with transparent cost/latency annotations.
- Accounting & safety: soft-fallback budget windows, lease burn-rate smoothing, and a safety throttler that prevents a tenant from exhausting cluster-level episodic reservoir.
- Telemetry: lease_allocations_total, lease_consumption_seconds, fallback_activations_total{reason}, episodic_reservoir_utilization_percent, per-tenant-burst_headroom_gauge. Added tracing spans for lease negotiation and fallback decision path.
- Config: feature gated under dedicated.autoscaling.episodicLeases.enabled=false by default; tuning knobs for epoch_length, max_lease_duration, per_tenant_epoch_quota, reservoir_size_pct.

Design notes and rationale:
- Short leases let us treat burst servicing as a different resource-class than reserved capacity; that reduces steady-state reservation pressure while preserving micro-SLOs.
- Immediate fallback is optimistic: route before retrying to avoid queuing-induced latency spikes. We attach TTL/cost metadata so callers and observability can distinguish fallback hits.
- We intentionally keep the episodic reservoir small and conservative in default values to avoid surprising sustained cost increases.

Commits summary:
- Add episodic lease controller and persistence layer (4 commits)
- Add fallback router and policy evaluator (2 commits)
- Telemetry + tracing additions (1 commit)
- Configuration + helm values (1 commit)
- Integration tests and e2e fixture (2 commits)

Files changed (high level):
- pkg/autoscaler/*: allocator, store and reconciliation logic (~650 LOC)
- pkg/routing/*: fallback policy evaluator and routing glue (~180 LOC)
- pkg/telemetry/*: metrics and dashboards wiring (~40 LOC)
- integration-tests/*: deterministic burst replay and assertion harness (~220 LOC)
- docs/ops/episodic-leases.md: operator guidance and tuning playbook

Testing and CI:
- unit tests for allocator/store logic (go test coverage ~86% for new packages)
- integration test simulates 1000 tenant bursts across 3 nodes and validates reservoir invariants and fallback correctness
- load-run job recorded 95th/99th percentile tail reduction for burst requests in our perf lab: P95 latency - 28% vs baseline, P99 - 16%
- CI initially flagged a flake in an unrelated test; rerun pipeline completed green (full build + e2e smoke).

Observability and alerting changes:
- New dashboards: "Episodic Leases Overview" and "Lease Consumption by Tenant"
- Alerts: High Episodic Reservoir Utilization (>85% sustained 5m) and Increased Fallback Rate (>1% sustained 10m) with links to runbook.

Rollout plan:
- Feature-gated, off by default. Canary rollout to dedicated clusters: small -> medium -> fleet, starting with non-critical regions.
- Ops playbook added in docs/ops/episodic-leases.md; quick rollback toggles available via console and helm.

Backward compatibility and safety:
- No changes to existing reservation or warm-pool semantics unless feature enabled. Fallback paths preserve request semantics (cost/region/model variant annotated) and honor tenant-configured routing preferences.

Review conversation (highlights):
- Maya Singh: "Can we add a hard upper-bound on per-tenant epoch quotas to prevent noisy neighbors at cluster scale?"
  Evan Calder: "Added safety_clamp in lease_store and a default aggressiveness factor in config; also added unit tests demonstrating clamp behavior."
- Liam O'Connor: "Trace spans are great but can be high-cardinality. Can we toggle per-tenant tracing for leases?"
  Evan Calder: "Added a tracing sampling config and limited high-cardinality attributes on default path."
- Sofia Park: "Integration test looks solid; can we add a canary smoke that verifies fallback reasons are surfaced to billing?"
  Evan Calder: "Added a billing-annotation step and a short canary test that verifies fallback annotations are included in the cost blob."
- Approvals: Maya, Liam approved after changes; Sofia approved after canary test addition.

Follow-ups (planned separate PRs):
- Cross-cluster episodic lease peering for geo-local bursts (ENG-4878).
- Cost modeling tool to convert lease activations into expected monthly spend (ENG-4891).

Related work and references:
- See design doc: https://linear.app/redwood/issue/ENG-4829/episodic-lease-controller-design
- Prior art: warm-pool warmlets, burst credits (see PRs pr-81502, pr-70333 for historical context).

Summary: This PR adds an opt-in episodic leasing layer and an immediate fallback controller to improve micro-burst tail latency while limiting long-term reserved capacity growth. It is gated, tested, and includes observability and operator guidance for safe rollouts.
